Scripts¶

Scripts

  • define the test sequence and operating modes of the test being run

  • are in human readable JSON file format

    • JSON is used so that non-programmers may be able to read/edit [1] the script without requiring a programming background. This is useful in development or emergency situations.

  • extend JSON a little bit, by allowing comments, any line beginning with // is a comment. This allows the script to be documented

The script has the following sections,

{
  "subs": {
  },
  "info": {
  },
  "config": {
  },
  "tests": [
  ]
}

subs¶

This is a section of User configurable substitutions for variables in the script. For example, if there was a test limit that could have two values, the values can be listed as a subs field and the user can select which one to use.

In a production environment, operators are not typically allowed to arbitrarily change values of test limits or any other setup. However, in an engineering lab, or new product ramp environment, having an easy method to change some parameters might be useful. This feature does not have to be used.

Only (logged in) users with a certain role privileges can access the Test Configuration page, and thus access to GUI controls that use the subs feature. Otherwise subs are used to create a Traveller, which stores the subs used.

subs are useful for generating Travellers.

Here is a full example of what subs section could look like (taken from example prod_1.scr),

"subs": {
  // Each item here is described by,
  // "<subs_name>":
  //   "title": "<title>",
  //   "type" : "<str|num>",
  //   "widget": "<textinput|select>",
  //   "regex": <"regex">,  // only for widget == textinput,
  //                           the field is valid when the regex is satisfied;
  //                           Validate enables once all fields are valid,
  //                           Start Testing enables after a successful Validate
  //   "choices": [<choice1>, <choice2>, ...],  // only for widget == select
  //   "default": <default>,
  //   "subs": // inner dependant subs
  //           { <key1> : { "subs_name1": {"val": <>, "type": "<str|num>" }, ...},
  //             <key2> : { "subs_name1": {"val": <>, "type": "<str|num>" }, ...}
  //           }
  // }
  //
  // Rules:
  // 1. key must not have any spaces or special characters
  //
  "Lot": {
    "title": "Lot (format #####)",
    "type" : "str", "widget": "textinput", "regex": "^\\d{5}$", "default": "95035"
  },
  "Loc": {
    "title": "Location",
    "type" : "str", "widget": "select", "choices": ["canada/ontario/milton",
                                                    "us/newyork/buffalo"],
    // inner dependant substitutions based on user input
    "subs" : {"canada/ontario/milton": { "TST000Min": { "val": 0.1, "type": "num" }},
              "us/newyork/buffalo":    { "TST000Min": { "val": 0.2, "type": "num" }}
    }
  },
  "TST000Max": {
    "title": "TST000 Max Attenuation (db)",
    "type" : "num", "widget": "select", "choices": [9.0, 10.0, 11.0]
  },
  "TST000Enable": {
    "title": "TST000_Meas Enable",
    "type" : "str", "widget": "select", "choices": ["true", "false"]
  }
},

// and how it looks in the test item,
{"id": "TST000_Meas",     "enable": "%%TST000Enable", "args": {"min": "%%TST000Min", "max": "%%TST000Max"}},

key

  • the name of the variable to be replaced somewhere else in the script, for example, the variable could be in the info section

    • the variable in other sections, would be named "%%key"

    • the variable would be listed with double quotes, regardless of the variable type

  • key should not have any special characters in it, else bad things happen

  • keys are matched whole, so "%%Lot" and "%%LotSize" are two different subs

title

  • this is the title of the field to be presented to the Operator in the Test Configuration page

  • if there is a specific format of the variable expected, that should be indicated in the title

type

  • indicates type of variable that is ultimately required in the final JSON version of the script

  • string (str) and number (num) (covers float and ints) are the only options

  • a num value must be a number, for example 9 or -0.5, otherwise Validate fails

  • a str value is used as typed; quotes and other special characters are kept as text

widget

  • the type of GUI widget to present to the Operator in the Test Configuration page

  • textinput is a generic text input box, which will be populated by the default field

  • select is a drop down selection menu

regex

  • used only for textinput widget

  • used to validate the Operator entered correct information

  • this is optional field

  • when every field is valid the Validate button is enabled, and after a successful Validate the Start Testing button is enabled

default

  • sets the default value for textinput widget

  • optional

Inner Subs¶

Inner subs allow one User sub to be able to set multiple other subs. An example is shown in the subs section above. In the above example, when Location is selected by the user, TST000Min is assigned a value depending on the Location selected.

From the example,

"Loc": {
  "title": "Location",
  "type" : "str", "widget": "select", "choices": ["canada/ontario/milton",
                                                  "us/newyork/buffalo"],
  "subs" : {"canada/ontario/milton": { "TST000Min": { "val": 0.1, "type": "num" }},
            "us/newyork/buffalo":    { "TST000Min": { "val": 0.2, "type": "num" }}
  }
},

// used in a test item
{"id": "TST000_Meas", "args": {"min": "%%TST000Min", "max": "%%TST000Max"}},

  • The keys of the inner subs (canada/ontario/milton, us/newyork/buffalo) are the values the Operator can pick, and must match the choices exactly.

  • Each value maps to one or more inner subs, given as "<key>": {"val": <value>, "type": "<str|num>"}.

    • <key> is used in the script as "%%<key>", the same as any other sub.

    • type works as described for type above; for num the quotes around "%%<key>" are removed.

  • Inner subs are not shown on the Test Configuration page; the Operator only picks Location. Here, picking us/newyork/buffalo makes the test item "args": {"min": 0.2, ...}.

  • An inner sub key must not also be a key of the top level subs section.

  • Every choice should list every inner sub. If the picked value has no entry, "%%TST000Min" is left in the script and Validate fails with ERROR: script subs problem.

  • Only one level is supported, an inner sub cannot have its own subs.

  • A Travellers stores only the Operator’s picks; the inner subs are applied again when the Traveller is scanned.

info¶

This section is a list of fields that correspond to fields that exist in the backend database and are typically used for database searches.

You cannot add or delete fields from this section. If there are missing fields, an error will occur downstream as the result record is checked to have these fields. New fields can be added, but that requires a request to customize the backend database. See TBD.

Note that the example here, two fields are using the subs section to get their values from the Operator in the Test Configuration page.

"info": {
  "product": "widget_1",
  "bom": "B00012-001",
  // list fields present user choice or fill in
  "lot": "%%Lot",
  "location": "%%Loc",
  // "config": "optional"
},

product - 32 character length field.

bom - 32 character length field. Note bom stands for Bill of Materials.

lot - 16 character length field.

location - 128 character length field.

config - (optional) 16 character length field.

Defining rules and a naming convention for these fields will help you later when you need to make database searches for specific sets of results. This is important.

config¶

This section sets required variables that Prism uses to drive the test script.

"config": {
  "fail_fast": true,
  "drivers": ["public.prism.drivers.fake.hwdrv_fake"]
},

fail_fast

  • this directive tells Prism whether to stop the test script on the first occurrence of a failed test

  • this directive can be overridden by the directive in the options section of the tests section - in other words, here it has the least priority

  • it is recommended fail_fast be set to true.

    • Often tests are interdependent, and if one test fails, it often means other tests will fail that depended on that particular function. What happens then is a cascade of failed tests which might obscure the root failure.

    • If tests are mutually exclusive, it may be advantageous to set fail_fast to false.

drivers

  • this is a list of drivers to start when the script it loaded

  • the dot notation is specifying a directory path to the python file to read

  • every script must have a driver. A fake driver is available in the case where you don’t want/need a real driver, for example, in development of code

  • See Drivers

tests¶

This section has a list of test definitions

  • each definition has fields module, options, items

  • items has fields id, enable, fail, and args

Consider the following test section, which only has ONE test definition in the JSON list. An example of more than one test definition will be shown later.

See public/prism/scripts/example/prod_v0/tst00xx.py for usage.

"tests": [
  {
    "module": "public.prism.scripts.example.prod_v0.tst00xx",
    "options": {
      "fail_fast": false
      // add more key/value as required
    },
    "items": [
      {"id": "TST0xxSETUP",           "enable": true },
      {"id": "TST000_Meas",           "enable": true, "args": {"min": 0, "max": "%%TST000Max"},
                                      "fail": [ {"fid": "TST000-0", "msg": "Component apple R1"},
                                                {"fid": "TST000-1", "msg": "Component banana R1"}] },
      {"id": "TST002_Skip",           "enable": false },
      {"id": "TST0xxTEARDOWN",        "enable": true }
    ]
  }
]

module

  • a dot notation path to the Python code that is associated with this test definition

options

  • a list of fields assigned values that persist over the execution life of the test item definition

  • Prism key words,

    • fail_fast overrides fail_fast in the config section

    • enable (defaults to true) when set to false, disables all tests in items

    • timeout seconds allowed for each test item, default 10 seconds (ResultAPI.TESTITEM_TIMEOUT in public/prism/api.py). A test item that runs longer is recorded as TIMEOUT, which is a fail.

  • add fields here as your application requires

  • these options fields are available programmatically to each test items

    • for example, you could have a global value assigned here that any test items can access

items

  • a list of test items, at least one

  • the system will execute these tests in order

  • Validate checks that every id is a function in module, args and options are objects, and any timeout is a positive number

    • id - A unique identifier of the test, which is also the Python (class) function name in module.

    • enable - true or false, can be omitted if always enabled

    • timeout - seconds allowed for this test item, overrides options timeout

    • args - a list of key/value pairs of any name/value required by your application

      • in the example shown, min and max keys are used and assigned values

      • note that max is using a subs entry

    • fail - a list of failure messages to present to the Operator and to store in the result database

      • These failure modes are accessed programmatically by your test code, see TBD

      • fid - a unique ID for this failure mode

      • msg - message to show operator, at most 64 characters, a short hint like "3V_OUT low: check U7 R49"

      • the test code attaches it to the result with ctx.record.fail_msg(ctx.item.fail[0]) when a measurement fails, see Binning Failures. Without that call the fail list is never shown

    • any other field your test code needs, for example "name": "V5V", "min": 4900, "max": 5100, read in the program as ctx.item.min. Fields on the item itself are easier to read than fields inside args, see Script Design

Script Design¶

A script is a list of tests, with their limits. Keep it readable by a person who is not a programmer.

When a test fails in production, and only a limit has to change, a production or test technician should be able to open the script, find the test, and change the limit. They should not need a programmer, and they should not need to read Python.

So,

  • everything the test does is in the Python program: which BOND pin is read, the divider ratio, the order of the steps, the commands sent to the DUT, the settle times

  • the script only says which tests run and with what limits: id, enable, timeout, min/max, fail, and a few other values a technician may change, such as a firmware file name or a hardware version

A good script looks like this,

"items": [
  {"id": "BLT000_SETUP",    "enable": true },
  {"id": "BLT100_voltage",  "enable": true, "name": "V5V",  "min": 4900, "max": 5100 },
  {"id": "BLT100_voltage",  "enable": true, "name": "V3V3", "min": 3200, "max": 3400 },
  {"id": "BLT100_voltage",  "enable": true, "name": "V1V8", "min": 1725, "max": 1875 },

  // disabled: Pogo board schematic error on VIN, see ECO-123
  {"id": "BLT100_voltage",  "enable": false, "name": "VIN", "min": 11800, "max": 12200 },

  {"id": "BLT200_program",  "enable": true, "file": "bootloader-1.2.hex", "timeout": 30 },
  {"id": "BLT300_fw_check", "enable": true, "version": "1.2" },
  {"id": "BLT990_TEARDOWN", "enable": true }
]

  • each line is one test, and the limits are on the line

  • put fields on the item itself ("min": 4900), not in args, so the line is easy to read

  • a comment says why a test is disabled

  • a fail message is a terse hint for the operator or repair technician, at most 64 characters, like "3V_OUT low: check U7 R49". Not the full list of parts a test covers, that belongs in the coverage analysis, see PCBA Test Coverage

  • the same test may run more than once, with a different name, when only the limits change, BLT100_voltage above. Each run must record a different measurement name, here the name. Only the first copy of a repeated id can be the target of _next.

And its program keeps the details, written out plainly,

# BOND header and pin of each rail, and the Pogo board divider (DUT mV = ADC mV * rdivf)
VOLTAGE_MAP = {
    "V5V":  {"hdr": 2, "pin": 16, "rdivf": 1.0},
    "V3V3": {"hdr": 3, "pin": 13, "rdivf": 1.0},
    "V1V8": {"hdr": 2, "pin": 14, "rdivf": 1.0},
    "VIN":  {"hdr": 2, "pin": 15, "rdivf": 3.0},
}

def BLT100_voltage(self):
    """ Measure a rail voltage, see VOLTAGE_MAP

        {"id": "BLT100_voltage", "enable": true, "name": "V5V", "min": 4900, "max": 5100 },
    """
    ctx = self.item_start()  # always first line of test

    if ctx.item.name not in self.VOLTAGE_MAP:
        self.logger.error(f"invalid voltage name {ctx.item.name}")
        self.item_end(ResultAPI.RECORD_RESULT_INTERNAL_ERROR)
        return

    rail = self.VOLTAGE_MAP[ctx.item.name]
    response = self.bond.bond_max_hdr_adc(rail["hdr"], rail["pin"])
    if not response["success"]:
        self.logger.error(response)
        self.item_end(ResultAPI.RECORD_RESULT_INTERNAL_ERROR)
        return

    value = response["result"]["mV"] * rail["rdivf"]
    _, result, bullet = ctx.record.measurement(ctx.item.name, value, ResultAPI.UNIT_MILLIVOLTS,
                                               min=ctx.item.min, max=ctx.item.max)
    self.log_bullet(bullet)
    self.item_end(result)  # always last line of test

Keep the program simple¶

Production test code is maintained for the life of the product, often by people who did not write it. Code that is easy to follow is better than code that is short.

  • write one test item method for each test, with its steps in order in the method

  • call the driver (self.bond.bond_max_hdr_adc(...)) and ctx.record.measurement(...) directly. Don’t wrap them in your own layer of helper classes or functions

  • hard code what doesn’t change in production, such as BOND pins, divider ratios, DUT commands and settle times, in the program, in a table like VOLTAGE_MAP or in the method

  • some repeated code between test items is fine, when it keeps each test item readable on its own

A reader should be able to follow a test item from top to bottom without opening another file or class, other than the drivers and the Prism APIs. So,

  • the program is one class that inherits only from TestItem. No base classes or mixins, and no shared module of test items. When two programs have the same setup or teardown item, each program has its own copy

  • call the drivers in the test item, check response["success"], and on a failure log it, end the item and return, as BLT100_voltage above. No fixture class around BOND, and no looking up pins by signal name in another module

  • record with ctx.record.measurement(name, value, ResultAPI.UNIT_MILLIVOLTS, min=..., max=...) and self.log_bullet(bullet), with the measurement name written out in full. The units are the ResultAPI.UNIT_* constants in public/prism/api.py: write the constant in each call (ResultAPI.UNIT_MILLIVOLTS), with no map, alias or short names of your own for them

  • handle each error where it happens: log, self.item_end(result), return. No context managers or decorators that turn exceptions into results, and no exception classes of your own to jump out of a test item. Use try only around the one call that can raise, such as opening a serial port

  • a test item that uses the result of an earlier one (saved in self) checks that it is there, and ends with RECORD_RESULT_INTERNAL_ERROR and a log message naming the item it needs when it is not

  • small pure functions in the program are fine, for example a checksum or a unit conversion, as long as they don’t call a driver or record anything

  • a library for the DUT’s own protocol (its command link) can be a separate module, the same as a driver. It doesn’t record measurements or call BOND

The examples in public/prism/scripts/example are written this way, for example BOND_v0/bond_P00xx.py.

Don’t wrap the recording and error handling into a “step” object, for example,

# Don't: the reader has to find Step, meas() and the UNITS map to know what is recorded
def T105a_3v_out(self):
    ctx = self.item_start()
    with self.step(ctx, "T1-05a") as t:
        t.meas("v3v_out", self.fx.adc_mv("J6_1") / 1000, "V", ctx.item.min, ctx.item.max)
    self.item_end(t.result)

Write it out,

def T105a_3v_out(self):
    """ +3V_OUT at J6.1, BOND HDR1 pin 13

        {"id": "T105a_3v_out", "enable": true, "min": 2940, "max": 3060 },
    """
    ctx = self.item_start()  # always first line of test

    response = self.bond.bond_max_hdr_adc(1, 13)
    if not response["success"]:
        self.logger.error(response)
        self.item_end(ResultAPI.RECORD_RESULT_INTERNAL_ERROR)
        return

    _, result, bullet = ctx.record.measurement("T105a_v3v_out", response["result"]["mV"],
                                               ResultAPI.UNIT_MILLIVOLTS,
                                               min=ctx.item.min, max=ctx.item.max)
    self.log_bullet(bullet)
    self.item_end(result)  # always last line of test

Don’t,

  • put lists of steps or actions in the script, for example "actions": [{"dac": "J3", "mv": 1000}, {"sleep": 0.05}, {"adc": "J3", "min": 880, ...}]. The script becomes a program, and the test code becomes an interpreter for it

  • put expressions, formulas, DUT commands or BOND pin numbers in the script

  • use one generic test item for unrelated tests, with the script choosing what it does

  • put layers between the test item and the drivers or ctx.record.measurement: base classes, fixture classes, step objects, meas()/check() helpers, unit maps

  • generate the script from another program or repo. The script in your scripts repo is the one that is changed, by hand, when a limit changes

[1]

Scripts CAN BE LOCKED DOWN so that a production user cannot change them. Locking down the Prism is covered TBD.
